title: Lifting with depression
summary: NH gives advice to a depressed viewer: avoid a caloric deficit, make consistency the top priority by training daily and leaving when drained, accept poor sleep and plan around it, and let training gradually restore metabolism, sleep and mood in a virtuous circle before focusing on bodybuilding goals.
claims: Training has a massive influence on mental health
He is neurotypical but has had dark periods, and lifting is what got his life under control
He will train until he dies; it is as essential to him as breathing or drinking water
He rejects the tough-it-up view: depression is brain chemistry, but you can still influence it and remain captain of the boat
If you are depressed, don't run a caloric deficit; eat at maintenance rather than bulking
If you cannot yet keep a routine, build it in small steps: shower, get dressed, take a two-minute walk, then add more
He is not fully in favour of psychiatric medication, which he sees as a crutch; if it works, keep it, but if not, consider building a life without it
Lifting brings endorphins and dopamine, makes you more social and reduces anxiety
For depressed lifters consistency is priority one; train every day even if it means fewer gains, because it structures your life
When you are drained, go home: dragging out sessions into junk volume makes the gym a chore and makes coming back harder
With poor sleep, don't take sleeping pills or try to force more sleep; accept it and organise training around reduced recovery
Consistency plus whatever sleep and food you get will raise your metabolism, which then improves sleep and training in a virtuous circle
Non-depressed lifters should focus on training and recovery and not obsess over metabolism or low testosterone; depressed lifters should do the opposite
First get stable, around a six out of ten every day, then focus on becoming a better bodybuilder
